title: Iced Kenkey
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Leftover kenkey blended with ice-cold water, sugar and evaporated milk to about the consistency of rice water.
longDesc: Iced kenkey is what happens to yesterday's kenkey, and it is one of the best cheap street drinks in West Africa — a cold, sour, milky, faintly grainy thing sold from coolers all over Ghana. A cup of leftover kenkey goes into a blender with half a cup of ice-cold water, a tablespoon of sugar and a third of a cup of evaporated milk, and the target is about the consistency of rice water. No cooking, no fermenting: the sourness is already there from the kenkey. Her own note is that it is an acquired taste for Westerners.
steps: Blend it with the ice-cold water.
Add the sugar and the evaporated milk.
Blend until it reaches about the consistency of rice water.
chefTips: About the consistency of rice water is the cue — pourable and slightly thick, not a smoothie and not a drink you could mistake for milk.
Ice-cold water, not room temperature. It is served cold and there is no cooking stage to lose heat from.
Use kenkey that is a day old. Fresh warm kenkey is for eating; the leftover ball is what this drink exists for.
Evaporated milk rather than fresh. It is sweeter and thicker and it is what is actually used in Ghana.
Sieve it if you want it smooth. Street versions are left slightly grainy and that is part of the character.
Her honest note, worth passing on: it is an acquired taste for Westerners. Sour fermented corn, milk and sugar is an unfamiliar combination if you did not grow up with it.
No fermentation step here at all — the sourness comes ready-made in the kenkey, which is why this entry needs no fermentation cue of its own.
commonMistakes: Blending it to a thin liquid or a thick paste rather than rice-water consistency.
Over-sweetening — a tablespoon for two servings is the printed amount.
sources: Adapted from 'Recipe #15: Iced Kenkey', betumiblog.blogspot.com, 9 September 2009. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Fran'. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS). Yield as printed on one fetch: 'Enough for 1-2 people'.
Ingredients exactly as printed: 1 cup kenkey (leftover); 1/2 cup ice cold water; 1 tablespoon sugar; 1/3 cup evaporated milk.
THE CONSISTENCY CUE, as printed: 'about the consistency of rice water'. That is the only cue the recipe gives and it is the one that matters — see GHA045 for rice water itself.
DESCRIPTION, as printed: 'a popular inexpensive snack/street food sold throughout much of Ghana'.

NO FERMENTATION STEP: this drink assembles already-made kenkey, so it carries no fermentation of its own. That is why it is publishable where several other Ghanaian fermented preparations in the research were refused — the fermentation happened in the kenkey, which is documented at GHA037.

A FULLER DESCRIPTION from a different post by the same author, 'Culinary entrepreneurship in Ghana', betumiblog.blogspot.com, 18 June 2010, byline 'Fran': it calls the drink 'a refreshing traditional sweetened fermented corn and milk drink known as ice kenkey', and adds that it is 'an acquired taste for Westerners'. That honest caveat is reproduced in the tips.
The post lists 'Recipe #12: Ga Kenkey' and a 'Fante kenkey reference' as its prerequisites — see GHA037 and GHA038.
storage: Same day. It separates and sours further.
healthBenefits: Carries the lactic acid bacteria of the fermented kenkey it is made from.
Evaporated milk adds calcium, protein and vitamin D.
Rehydrating and cooling in hot weather.
Uses up leftovers that would otherwise be wasted.
culturalNote: Iced kenkey is sold from insulated flasks by hawkers and in sachets from shops, and it is the clearest example in Ghanaian food of nothing going to waste — yesterday's staple becomes today's cold drink. The sourness that makes it strange to outsiders is exactly what makes it refreshing in Accra heat.
